subject: ela
skillName: Develop and strengthen writing through planning, revising, editing
intro: Each problem gives you a short draft paragraph. Read the whole draft, then make the one decision that improves the writing the most. Write your answer and be ready to explain it against the whole paragraph.

items.prompt: Read this draft paragraph: "Our school should start a recycling club. A recycling club would be a great idea for our school. Many students throw away bottles and paper every day. Last year over five hundred plastic bottles ended up in the trash. A club could place bins in every hallway and teach students how to sort waste." One sentence weakens the paragraph by adding nothing new. Which sentence should the writer cut, and why?
items.answer: Cut the second sentence, "A recycling club would be a great idea for our school," because it only repeats the first sentence's point and adds no new support.

steps: Identify the main idea: the school should start a recycling club.
The first sentence states that idea clearly.
The second sentence repeats the same claim in different words and offers no reason, evidence, or new detail.
The remaining sentences each add support (students waste bottles and paper, the five hundred bottle figure, what the club would do), so they belong.
Cutting the repeated sentence tightens the paragraph without losing any support.

items.prompt: Read this draft paragraph: "The water cycle moves water around the Earth. First, water falls to the ground as rain or snow. The sun heats water in oceans and lakes, turning it into vapor that rises into the air. As the vapor cools, it forms clouds. Then it falls again as rain or snow." The sentences are out of logical order. What is the best reordering of the four steps, and why?
items.answer: Reorder so evaporation comes first: the sun heats water into vapor, the vapor cools into clouds, then it falls as rain or snow, and that falling water reaches the ground. The current draft starts with rain falling before any water has risen, which is out of sequence.

steps: List the steps the draft names: water falls as rain or snow, the sun turns water to vapor, vapor cools into clouds, it falls again.
A cycle has no true beginning, but the steps must follow cause to effect: water must rise before it can cool, and clouds must form before precipitation falls.
The draft puts 'water falls to the ground' before the sun has evaporated any water, breaking the logical flow.
The clear order is evaporation, then cooling into clouds, then precipitation falling to the ground.
Reordering this way makes each step follow logically from the one before it.

items.prompt: Read this draft paragraph: "The class trip to the museum was fun. The bus was fun. The exhibits were fun. The lunch in the courtyard was fun. Everyone said it was a fun day." A reader says the writing is dull because one word is overused. Which single revision strengthens the paragraph most, and why? Choose between: replacing each 'fun' with a different precise word that fits that part of the day, OR adding a sentence that says the day was very fun.
items.answer: Replace each repeated 'fun' with a precise word that fits that moment, such as 'the bumpy bus ride was lively,' 'the dinosaur exhibits were fascinating,' and 'the courtyard lunch was relaxing.' Adding another 'fun' sentence would only repeat the weak word again.

steps: The paragraph repeats 'fun' five times, which makes it vague and flat.
Adding a sentence that says the day was 'very fun' repeats the same weak word and adds no new information.
Replacing each 'fun' with a precise word gives the reader a clear, specific picture of each part of the day.
Precise word choice fixes the real weakness, the overused vague word.
Therefore the strongest revision is to swap in varied, exact words rather than pile on more 'fun'.

items.prompt: Read this draft paragraph: "Dogs make excellent pets for families. They are loyal and love to play. A dog can be trained to follow commands and protect a home. My neighbor painted his fence bright green last summer. Many families say their dog feels like a member of the family." One sentence does not fit the topic. Which sentence should the writer remove during revision, and why?
items.answer: Remove the sentence "My neighbor painted his fence bright green last summer," because it is about a fence, not about dogs as family pets, so it does not support the paragraph's topic.

steps: Find the topic: dogs make excellent pets for families.
Check each sentence against that topic.
The sentences about loyalty, playfulness, training, protection, and feeling like family all support the topic.
The sentence about the neighbor painting a fence green has nothing to do with dogs as pets.
Removing the off-topic fence sentence keeps the paragraph focused on its main idea.

items.prompt: Read this draft note from a writer: "I have rewritten the same paragraph four times. Each time I only change one or two words, but my classmates still say they cannot tell what my main point is. The order of my ideas jumps around, and I never actually state my opinion. I am running out of single words to swap." What should the writer do next, and why?
items.answer: The writer should stop swapping single words and instead rewrite the paragraph with a new approach: plan the main point first, state the opinion clearly, and order the ideas logically. Small word changes have already failed four times because the real problems are focus and organization.

steps: Notice that the writer has tried small word fixes four times with no success.
The stated problems are bigger than word choice: an unclear main point, jumping ideas, and a missing opinion.
Word swaps cannot fix missing focus or poor organization.
When small fixes keep failing, the right move is to rewrite or try a new approach.
So the writer should replan and rewrite the paragraph, stating the opinion and ordering ideas, instead of changing more words.

items.prompt: Read this draft paragraph: "Exercise is good for you. Exercise is good. Running, swimming, and biking all build strength. When you exercise, your heart and lungs get stronger. People who move every day often feel happier too." The paragraph has both a repeated weak sentence and strong support. What is the single best revision, and why?
items.answer: Cut the repeated second sentence, "Exercise is good," because it only echoes the first sentence and adds no new support, while the sentences about specific activities, the heart and lungs, and feeling happier all develop the topic and should stay.

steps: The first two sentences make the same claim, so one is redundant.
The second sentence, 'Exercise is good,' is the weaker, shorter repeat and adds nothing new.
The remaining sentences give specific support: named activities, body effects, and mood.
Cutting only the repeated sentence removes the weakness while keeping all the real support.
Therefore the best single revision is to delete 'Exercise is good.'

items.prompt: Read this draft paragraph that claims a position but never explains it: "Schools should start later in the morning. A later start would help students. It would be a good change. Most people would agree with this. I really think it is a good idea." The paragraph repeats its opinion but gives no reasons. Which revision strengthens it most, and why?
items.answer: Replace the repeated opinion sentences with sentences that add real reasons, such as "Teenagers need more sleep to focus, and a later start would let them rest, arrive alert, and earn better grades." The draft restates its opinion four times without evidence, so adding reasons is what it needs.

steps: Identify the claim: schools should start later.
Notice that every sentence after the first just repeats that the idea is good.
Repeating an opinion does not develop a paragraph; it needs supporting reasons or evidence.
Adding concrete reasons, such as students needing sleep and arriving more alert, gives the claim support.
So the strongest revision swaps the empty restatements for real reasons.

items.prompt: Read this draft paragraph: "me and my brother builded a treehouse last summer. we worked on it for three weekends. their were many nails and boards to use. finally, we climbed up and ate lunch inside it." The writer is now at the editing stage. List the convention errors to fix without changing the meaning.
items.answer: Fix: capitalize the first word of each sentence; change "me and my brother" to "My brother and I"; change "builded" to "built"; change "their" to "there." The corrected first sentence reads: "My brother and I built a treehouse last summer." These edits fix conventions without changing the meaning.

steps: This is editing, so look only for surface convention errors, not content changes.
Capitalization: each sentence should begin with a capital letter.
Pronoun and order: 'me and my brother' as the subject should be 'My brother and I.'
Verb form: 'builded' is not standard; the correct past tense is 'built.'
Word confusion: 'their were' should be 'there were,' the word that shows existence.
Apply each fix while keeping the writer's meaning the same.

items.prompt: Read this draft paragraph: "The volcano erupted in the morning. Ash covered the nearby town. Scientists had warned people the day before. Many families left their homes early. Because of the warning, almost everyone reached safety." A classmate says the events are hard to follow because they are not in time order. What is the best reordering, and why?
items.answer: Order the events by time: scientists warned people the day before, then families left their homes early, then the volcano erupted in the morning and ash covered the town, and because of the warning almost everyone reached safety. The draft mentions the eruption before the earlier warning and evacuation.

steps: List the events and when they happened: the warning (day before), families leaving (early), the eruption (morning), ash covering the town, people reaching safety.
The draft opens with the eruption, but the warning and the evacuation happened earlier.
Putting events in time order helps the reader follow cause and effect.
Correct order: warning first, then evacuation, then eruption and ash, then the safe outcome.
This reordering makes the sequence clear and logical.

items.prompt: Read this draft paragraph: "Reading every night helps you in many ways. It builds your vocabulary. Reading is a good thing that everyone should try to do more of because it is helpful and good for you in lots of different kinds of ways every single day. It also improves your focus." One sentence is wordy and repetitive. Which revision improves clarity most, and why?
items.answer: Replace the long third sentence with a concise one that adds a real benefit, such as "It can also relax your mind before sleep." The original sentence just repeats that reading is 'helpful and good' in many words without adding new information.

steps: Find the weak sentence: the long third sentence piles up vague phrases like 'helpful and good' and 'lots of different kinds of ways.'
It repeats the paragraph's main idea without adding a new benefit.
Clear writing trades wordy repetition for precise, specific support.
Replacing it with one concise sentence naming a new benefit improves clarity and keeps the paragraph focused.
Therefore the best revision cuts the wordy repeat and adds a precise point.

items.prompt: Read this draft paragraph: "Our town needs a new library. The old one is too small. Shelves are crammed and there is nowhere to sit and read. A larger library could hold more books and add quiet study rooms. Pizza is my favorite food. Students would have a calm place to do homework after school." Identify the sentence to cut and explain why the others stay.
items.answer: Cut "Pizza is my favorite food," because it is off topic and does not support the argument for a new library. The other sentences all explain why the town needs a bigger library, so they stay.

steps: Identify the topic: the town needs a new, larger library.
Check each sentence: the small old library, crammed shelves, more books and study rooms, and a calm homework place all support the topic.
'Pizza is my favorite food' has nothing to do with libraries.
An off-topic sentence weakens focus and should be removed during revision.
Cutting the pizza sentence keeps the paragraph on its main idea.

items.prompt: Read this draft paragraph: "The team practiced hard all season. They ran drills every morning. They watched film of other teams. They lifted weights. They practiced a lot." A reader says the last sentence is weak. What is the single best revision, and why? Choose between cutting the last sentence because it repeats the first, OR replacing it with a specific new detail about their practice.
items.answer: Replace the last sentence with a specific new detail, such as "They even stayed late to perfect their plays." Cutting it is acceptable, but the strongest revision adds new, precise support, while 'They practiced a lot' only repeats the first sentence's idea.

steps: The last sentence, 'They practiced a lot,' repeats the first sentence, 'The team practiced hard all season.'
A repeated vague sentence adds no new information.
Cutting it removes the weakness but adds nothing.
Replacing it with a specific detail, like staying late to perfect plays, both removes the repetition and strengthens the support.
So the best revision is to replace the weak sentence with a precise new detail.

items.prompt: Read this draft note from a writer planning an essay: "I wrote my whole essay before making any plan. Now my three reasons are scattered across different paragraphs, some sentences repeat, and my conclusion brings up a brand new idea that I never explained. Fixing one sentence at a time has not helped." What is the best next step, and why?
items.answer: The writer should go back and plan: make an outline that groups each reason in its own paragraph, removes the repeats, and keeps the conclusion to ideas already explained, then revise the draft to match the plan. The problems are organization and focus, which single-sentence fixes cannot solve.

steps: The listed problems are scattered reasons, repeated sentences, and a conclusion with an unexplained new idea.
These are organization and focus problems across the whole essay, not surface errors.
Fixing one sentence at a time has already failed.
The fix is to plan with an outline that organizes the reasons and then revise the draft to follow it.
Planning and reorganizing addresses the real, whole-draft weakness.

items.prompt: Read this draft paragraph: "My grandmother's garden is beautiful. There are roses. There are tomatoes. There are tall sunflowers that lean toward the sun. There are bees. There are also some green beans climbing a wooden fence." The sentences are choppy and repeat the same opener. Which revision improves the flow most, and why?
items.answer: Combine the choppy sentences into smoother ones that vary the structure, such as "My grandmother's garden is beautiful, with roses, tomatoes, and tall sunflowers that lean toward the sun, while bees hum near green beans climbing a wooden fence." This fixes the repeated 'There are' openers and the choppy flow.

steps: Notice the weakness: nearly every sentence begins 'There are,' making the writing choppy and repetitive.
Choppy, repetitive sentences interrupt the reader's flow.
Combining related items into longer, varied sentences improves sentence flow.
The combined version groups the plants and the bees smoothly and varies the sentence openings.
Therefore combining the choppy sentences is the strongest revision for flow.

items.prompt: Read this draft paragraph: "i visited washington d.c. in april. we saw the lincoln memorial and the capitol building. the cherry trees was blooming everywhere. me and my dad walked along the river. it were the best trip of my life." The writer is editing for conventions only. List each correction and the corrected paragraph, without changing the meaning.
items.answer: Corrections: capitalize sentence beginnings and proper nouns (I, Washington D.C., Lincoln Memorial, Capitol Building); 'trees was' becomes 'trees were'; 'me and my dad' becomes 'My dad and I'; 'it were' becomes 'it was.' Corrected: "I visited Washington D.C. in April. We saw the Lincoln Memorial and the Capitol Building. The cherry trees were blooming everywhere. My dad and I walked along the river. It was the best trip of my life."

steps: This is editing, so fix only conventions and keep the meaning.
Capitalization: start each sentence with a capital, capitalize 'I,' and capitalize proper nouns like Washington D.C., Lincoln Memorial, and Capitol Building.
Subject-verb agreement: 'trees was' should be 'trees were,' and 'it were' should be 'it was.'
Pronoun and order: 'me and my dad' as the subject should be 'My dad and I.'
Apply all fixes to produce the corrected paragraph with the same meaning.
